intro.en: A short route through the main gods and the three stories that hold the whole mythology together: the binding of the wolf, the death of Baldr, and the end of the world.

link.en: The world was built by the three sons of Borr; the first of them named is Óðinn.
Óðinn's strongest son, and the gods' defender against giants, is Þórr.
Þórr's companion on several journeys, and the gods' most troublesome member, is Loki.
The gods blamed Loki for the builder's bargain that put Freyja at risk; she is the next card.
Loki's own children were a danger too, and only one god dared feed the wolf: Týr.
Týr's courage is clearest in the binding of Fenrir.
Next comes the gods' worst loss: Óðinn's son Baldr.
Snorri calls Baldr's death the greatest misfortune among gods and men.
After Baldr, Loki is bound, and the next time all bonds break, it is the end.
Ragnarök is not quite the end: read on to the world renewed if you have a minute more.

intro.en: All the stories of the gods in one reading order, from the empty gap before the world to the green earth after the fire. Where the sources give an order, it is followed; elsewhere the order is a reading aid.

link.en: With the world built, the gods make people from two trees.
Next the gods' peace is broken by their first war, against the Vanir.
Völuspá follows the war with broken oaths, which Snorri explains through the builder of the gods' wall.
Þórr's hammer, used to pay the builder, is one of the treasures the dwarfs made for the gods.
Loki causes trouble again when he lures Iðunn and her apples out of Ásgarðr.
Þjazi's daughter Skaði then comes to Ásgarðr for revenge.
Snorri's next tale goes back to the peace with the Vanir, and the mead brewed from Kvasir's blood.
Another god longs for something in Jötunheimar: Freyr, who sees Gerðr.
The giants' lands are also where Þórr travels, most famously to Útgarða-Loki.
To make up for that journey, Þórr goes fishing for the serpent.
Next Þórr fights his first duel, with the giant Hrungnir.
Loki, caught by another giant, has to bring Þórr to Geirröðr without his hammer.
Once the hammer itself is stolen, and Þórr has to dress as a bride to get it back.
The gods also bind Loki's son, the wolf Fenrir.
Then the worst thing happens: Baldr dies.
At Ægir's feast Loki boasts of Baldr's death and insults every god.
After the feast the gods catch Loki and bind him.
He lies bound until all bonds break at Ragnarök.
After the fire, the earth rises again.
For the heroes' stories, which run alongside, start with Andvari's gold.

intro.en: Þórr's stories in one reading order, from the forging of his hammer to his last fight. No source gives the order of his journeys; where Snorri links two of them, that link is followed.

link.en: Þórr's hammer was one of the treasures the dwarfs made after Loki cut off Sif's hair.
The gods judged the hammer the best of all the treasures, because it was their greatest defence against the frost-giants.
On his journey east to Útgarða-Loki, Þórr used the hammer to bring his slaughtered goats back to life.
On that journey a farmer's son who cracked a goat's bone for the marrow became Þórr's servant.
Snorri says Þórr went fishing for the Miðgarðr serpent soon after he came home from Útgarðr.
Þjálfi is at Þórr's side again when the giant Hrungnir challenges Þórr to single combat.
Once Þórr had to face a giant without his hammer: Loki had promised Geirröðr to bring him unarmed.
In Þrymskviða the hammer itself is stolen, and Þórr has to dress as a bride to get it back.
Þórr's last fight is with the Miðgarðr serpent, at Ragnarök.
After the fire, says Vafþrúðnismál, Þórr's sons Móði and Magni will have Mjöllnir.

intro.en: Follow Andvari's gold and his cursed ring from an otter's ransom to the bottom of the Rhine, meeting everyone who held it on the way.

link.en: Loki took all of Andvari's gold, ring and all, to pay for an otter that was a man's son.
The ring Andvari cursed has its own name: Andvaranautr.
The first to keep the gold was Hreiðmarr, the otter's father.
He would share none of it with his sons Fáfnir and Reginn, and they killed him for it.
Fáfnir lay on the gold in the shape of a serpent; his brother Reginn fostered the boy who would kill him.
Reginn's foster-son was Sigurðr, son of Sigmundr.
Sigurðr killed Fáfnir from a pit and loaded the gold onto his horse Grani.
The birds also told Sigurðr of a valkyrie asleep on Hindarfjall.
Snorri calls the woman Sigurðr woke Brynhildr. Later she vowed to marry only the man who rode through the fire around her hall.
Sigurðr gave Brynhildr Andvari's ring, and Guðrún later used that ring to show who had really ridden through the fire.
After Sigurðr's death his widow Guðrún was married to King Atli.
Her brothers Gunnarr and Högni had taken the gold, and hid it in the Rhine before riding to Atli.
Högni rode with him, and laughed while his heart was cut out.
Their deaths at Atli's court end the story of the gold.
The gold, says Snorri, has never been found.

intro.en: Loki's three monstrous children, the gods' attempts to keep them down, and how everything breaks loose at the end of the world.

link.en: With the giantess Angrboða in Jötunheimar Loki had three children.
The first of them was the wolf Fenrir.
The second was the serpent Jörmungandr, which Óðinn threw into the sea around all lands.
The third was Hel, whom Óðinn threw into Niflheimr and gave power over those who die of sickness or old age.
The wolf the gods kept at home, until they had to bind him.
Loki himself caused the death of Baldr.
For Baldr's death the gods caught Loki and bound him in a cave.
Loki, like the wolf, lies bound until Ragnarök, when every fetter breaks.
Fenrir swallows Óðinn, Þórr kills the serpent and dies of its poison, and Loki and Heimdallr kill each other. After the fire, the earth rises again.
